title: Sprint 2 — Sequence: Request and Interaction Flows
description: Model interaction order, synchronous vs asynchronous communications, alternative flows, and error recovery using Mermaid sequence diagrams.

tickets.title: URL Shortening Request Flow
tickets.description:
### Scenario
Model the exact interaction order for creating short links and handling invalid inputs using a Mermaid sequence diagram.

### Primary Tab
**Sequence · Mermaid**

### Requirements
1. Define participants: Client, API Gateway, URL Service, and Database.
2. Model the successful creation flow: validation, unique hash generation, and database insertion.
3. Add an alternative branch (`alt ... else`) showing how malformed URLs are rejected.
4. Show the returned short URL payload and HTTP status codes.

### Acceptance Criteria
- The sequence diagram accurately displays both the successful creation path and the error validation branch.
tasks: Define participants: Client, URL Service, and Database.
Model the request to create a short URL with sequential step numbering.
Show the database write operation and returned short URL response.
Add an alternative flow branch for invalid or unreachable URLs.
learning_objectives: Learn Mermaid sequence diagram syntax (participants, arrows, activations, alt blocks).
Understand synchronous validation and error response branching.
Model state changes and status codes in interaction diagrams.
common_mistakes: Omitting the error/invalid URL alternative path.
Mislabeling asynchronous vs synchronous message arrows (`->>` vs `-->>`).
Directly connecting the client to the database without the application service.
hints: Use `autonumber` at the start of your sequence diagram for numbered steps.
Use `alt Invalid URL format` and `else Valid URL` blocks to illustrate branching logic.
Return `400 Bad Request` on invalid inputs and `201 Created` on success.

system_design.seq:
sequenceDiagram
  autonumber
  actor C as Client
  participant G as API Gateway
  participant S as URL Service
  participant R as Redis Cache
  participant D as PostgreSQL DB

  C->>+G: POST /api/v1/urls { "long_url": "https://example.com/item/1" }
  G->>+S: Forward create request
  alt Invalid URL format
    S-->>G: 400 Bad Request (Invalid URL syntax)
    G-->>C: 400 Bad Request
  else Valid URL
    S->>S: Generate Base62 hash (e.g. "x8k2Q")
    S->>+D: INSERT INTO urls (short_code, original_url, created_at)
    D-->>-S: 201 Inserted
    S->>+R: SET short_code -> original_url (TTL 7d)
    R-->>-S: OK
    S-->>-G: 201 Created { "short_code": "x8k2Q" }
    G-->>-C: 201 Created { "short_url": "https://yu.vr/x8k2Q" }
  end

notes.sequence:
## URL Shortening Flow
- Validates input format before generating hash.
- Dual-writes to PostgreSQL (durable) and Redis (fast cache warming).
- Handles invalid URL branches gracefully with 400 status.

solution.explanation: Demonstrates a comprehensive Mermaid sequence flow with input validation branching, Base62 hashing, database persistence, cache population, and status codes.
solution.approach: Mermaid sequence diagram with alt/else branching.

tickets.title: User Authentication Flow
tickets.description:
### Scenario
Model a secure authentication and token issuance workflow (JWT Access + Refresh tokens) between Client, Gateway, Auth Service, and User Database.

### Primary Tab
**Sequence · Mermaid**

### Requirements
1. Model Client, API Gateway, Authentication Service, and User Database.
2. Show credential verification (password hashing check) and token generation.
3. Include negative cases: incorrect credentials and expired/invalid tokens.
4. Clarify the boundary between authentication (login) and authorization (accessing protected resources).

### Acceptance Criteria
- Diagram covers successful login, credential failure, and token refresh cases.
tasks: Model Client, API Gateway, Authentication Service and User Database.
Show credential validation and token issuance (JWT Access & Refresh tokens).
Include incorrect credentials and expired-token failure cases.
Distinguish authentication from authorization in subsequent requests.
learning_objectives: Model token-based authentication (JWT + Refresh token rotation).
Understand error branches for 401 Unauthorized vs 403 Forbidden.
Diagram security lifecycles clearly using Mermaid.
common_mistakes: Storing or transmitting passwords in plaintext without hashing.
Failing to model expired token handling.
Conflating authentication (who you are) with authorization (what you can do).
hints: Use `alt Invalid credentials` to show the 401 Unauthorized branch.
Show the Auth Service issuing both an Access Token (short-lived) and a Refresh Token (long-lived).
Show the storage of active refresh tokens in a fast store like Redis.

system_design.seq:
sequenceDiagram
  autonumber
  actor C as Client
  participant G as API Gateway
  participant A as Auth Service
  participant D as User DB
  participant R as Token Cache (Redis)

  C->>+G: POST /api/v1/auth/login { email, password }
  G->>+A: Verify credentials
  A->>+D: SELECT id, password_hash, role FROM users WHERE email = ?
  D-->>-A: Return user record
  alt Invalid password / user not found
    A-->>G: 401 Unauthorized (Invalid credentials)
    G-->>C: 401 Unauthorized
  else Valid credentials
    A->>A: Verify bcrypt(password, hash)
    A->>A: Generate Access Token (JWT, 15m) & Refresh Token (UUID, 14d)
    A->>+R: SET refresh_token -> user_id (TTL 14d)
    R-->>-A: OK
    A-->>-G: 200 OK { access_token, refresh_token, expires_in: 900 }
    G-->>-C: 200 OK (Tokens received)
  end

  opt Accessing Protected Resource
    C->>+G: GET /api/v1/profile (Header: Bearer access_token)
    G->>G: Verify JWT signature & expiration
    alt Token Expired
      G-->>C: 401 Unauthorized (Token expired)
    else Valid Token
      G-->>-C: 200 OK { user profile data }
    end
  end

notes.sequence:
## Authentication & Authorization Flow
- Short-lived stateless JWT access tokens for API Gateway verification.
- Long-lived refresh tokens stored in Redis for revocation capability.
- Explicit branches for invalid credentials and expired tokens.

solution.explanation: Illustrates complete token issuance, password hash comparison, refresh token caching, and token expiration handling during protected resource access.
solution.approach: Stateless JWT access tokens with stateful refresh token verification.

tickets.title: E-commerce Order Placement
tickets.description:
### Scenario
Design the interaction sequence for e-commerce checkout involving inventory reservation, payment charging, order confirmation, and compensating transactions on failure.

### Primary Tab
**Sequence · Mermaid**

### Requirements
1. Model Client, Order Service, Inventory Service, and Payment Service.
2. Enforce inventory reservation before attempting payment processing.
3. Include payment success and failure branches.
4. Design compensating transactions: if payment fails or times out, release the reserved inventory.

### Acceptance Criteria
- Diagram accounts for partial failures and exhibits an explicit compensating rollback.
tasks: Model Client, Order Service, Inventory Service, and Payment Gateway.
Show inventory reservation prior to payment execution.
Include payment approval and payment decline branches.
Document compensation: release reserved inventory when payment fails.
learning_objectives: Master the Saga pattern (orchestration-based) and compensating transactions.
Prevent inventory leakage during distributed checkout workflows.
Model distributed partial failure states in sequence diagrams.
common_mistakes: Deducting inventory permanently before payment confirmation.
Failing to release held inventory when a payment provider declines or times out.
Omitting idempotency keys on order creation requests.
hints: Use temporary inventory holds (reservation status) rather than direct deletion of stock.
In the `else Payment Failed` block, show a message from Order Service to Inventory Service: `Compensate: Release hold`.
Use asynchronous event publishing for non-critical post-checkout steps like notifications.

system_design.seq:
sequenceDiagram
  autonumber
  actor C as Client
  participant O as Order Service
  participant I as Inventory Service
  participant P as Payment Gateway
  participant N as Notification Service

  C->>+O: POST /api/v1/orders { items, idempotency_key }
  O->>+I: Reserve inventory (item_ids, quantities)
  alt Insufficient stock
    I-->>O: Stock unavailable
    O-->>C: 409 Conflict (Items out of stock)
  else Stock reserved
    I-->>-O: Reservation successful (Hold 15m)
    O->>+P: Charge payment ($120.00)
    alt Payment failed / declined
      P-->>O: Payment declined (Insufficient funds)
      O->>+I: Compensate: Release reserved inventory
      I-->>-O: Hold released
      O-->>C: 402 Payment Required
    else Payment succeeded
      P-->>-O: Payment confirmed (txn_id: "tx_9921")
      O->>O: Mark order status = 'CONFIRMED'
      O->>+N: Publish OrderPlacedEvent (async)
      N-->>-O: Ack
      O-->>-C: 201 Created { order_id: "ord_101", status: "CONFIRMED" }
    end
  end

notes.sequence:
## E-commerce Checkout Sequence
- Step 1: Reserve inventory with temporary hold.
- Step 2: Charge payment gateway.
- Step 3: If payment fails, trigger compensating rollback to release inventory hold.
- Step 4: Asynchronously dispatch confirmation notification.

solution.explanation: Illustrates orchestrated distributed transaction with two-phase inventory reservation and compensating rollback upon payment failure.
solution.approach: Orchestrated Saga pattern with compensating actions.

tickets.title: Asynchronous Notification Delivery
tickets.description:
### Scenario
Model end-to-end asynchronous notification delivery through a message broker, showing immediate API acknowledgment, worker processing, retries, and dead-letter queue routing.

### Primary Tab
**Sequence · Mermaid**

### Requirements
1. Model API Service, Message Queue, Notification Worker, and Email Provider.
2. Return an immediate acknowledgment (`202 Accepted`) to the calling client.
3. Show the worker consuming the message and dispatching to the provider.
4. Detail the failure path: retry with backoff, and terminal routing to a Dead Letter Queue (DLQ).

### Acceptance Criteria
- The sequence diagram proves client requests do not block on external provider latency.
tasks: Model the API Service, Message Queue, Worker, and Third-Party Provider.
Show immediate acknowledgment (`202 Accepted`) after message enqueuing.
Add retry loop behavior when provider delivery experiences transient errors.
Show the terminal failure path routing the message to a Dead Letter Queue (DLQ).
learning_objectives: Understand asynchronous decoupling with message queues.
Model exponential backoff and retry limits in sequence diagrams.
Implement Dead Letter Queue (DLQ) architectures for unprocessable events.
common_mistakes: Holding the client HTTP connection open while the worker retries sending.
Dropping messages on provider failure instead of moving them to a DLQ.
Missing acknowledgment (ACK) mechanics from the worker to the queue.
hints: Return `202 Accepted` to the client immediately after enqueuing the message.
Use a `loop` block to indicate the worker retrying up to max attempts.
Send message to the DLQ only after retries are exhausted, then ACK the original queue.

system_design.seq:
sequenceDiagram
  autonumber
  actor P as Producer Service
  participant Q as Notification Queue (Kafka)
  participant W as Worker Pool
  participant E as Email Provider (SendGrid)
  participant D as Dead Letter Queue (DLQ)

  P->>+Q: Enqueue SendEmailEvent { to, template, data }
  Q-->>-P: 202 Accepted (job_id: "job_771")

  Note over Q,W: Asynchronous processing
  W->>+Q: Pull message
  Q-->>-W: Deliver SendEmailEvent
  W->>+E: Send email API request
  alt Provider Success (200 OK)
    E-->>W: 200 OK
    W->>Q: ACK message (remove from queue)
  else Provider Transient 5xx / Rate Limit
    E-->>-W: 503 Service Unavailable
    loop Retry with Exponential Backoff (1..3)
      W->>W: Wait backoff interval (2s, 4s, 8s)
      W->>E: Retry Send Email
    end
    alt Max Retries Exhausted
      W->>+D: Move poison message to DLQ
      D-->>-W: Stored in DLQ
      W->>Q: ACK original queue message
    end
  end

notes.sequence:
## Asynchronous Notification Sequence
- Non-blocking client response with 202 Accepted.
- Worker pulls from message queue and handles transient failures.
- Terminal failures safely preserved in DLQ for manual inspection or replay.

solution.explanation: Illustrates non-blocking job enqueuing, worker polling, retry loops with backoff, and dead-letter queue routing for resilient messaging.
solution.approach: Asynchronous queue processing with retry and DLQ pattern.

tickets.title: Ticket Booking Under Concurrent Demand
tickets.description:
### Scenario
Model high-concurrency ticket booking where multiple users attempt to reserve the same popular seat simultaneously. Handle distributed locking, temporary holds, and hold expiration.

### Primary Tab
**Sequence · Mermaid**

### Requirements
1. Model Client 1, Client 2, Booking Service, Distributed Lock (Redis), and Database.
2. Show simultaneous reservation attempts for the exact same seat.
3. Demonstrate distributed locking: the first requester succeeds; the second receives a conflict response.
4. Model payment timeout behavior and seat-release cleanup by a background worker.

### Acceptance Criteria
- Prevents duplicate reservations under concurrency and models hold expiration cleanly.
tasks: Model Client 1, Client 2, Booking Service, Distributed Lock (Redis), and DB.
Demonstrate simultaneous reservation requests for the same seat.
Show lock acquisition by User 1 and lock rejection (409 Conflict) for User 2.
Model timeout expiration and automatic seat release when payment is not completed.
learning_objectives: Learn distributed locking with Redis (Redlock / SET NX EX).
Prevent race conditions and double-booking in high-traffic applications.
Model TTL-based temporary holds and automated expiration cleanup.
common_mistakes: Allowing race conditions by checking and booking without atomic locks.
Failing to release holds when users abandon checkout.
Blocking all database tables rather than using row-level or distributed locks.
hints: Use `par` block in Mermaid to represent simultaneous requests from Client 1 and Client 2.
Show Redis atomic lock `SET lock:seat:{id} (NX, EX 10s)`.
Show a background worker releasing expired holds where `expires_at < NOW()`.

system_design.seq:
sequenceDiagram
  autonumber
  actor C1 as User 1
  actor C2 as User 2
  participant B as Booking Service
  participant R as Redis (Distributed Lock)
  participant D as Bookings DB
  participant W as Expiration Worker

  par Simultaneous Booking for Seat 42
    C1->>+B: POST /reserve { event_id: 10, seat_id: 42 }
    C2->>+B: POST /reserve { event_id: 10, seat_id: 42 }
  end

  B->>+R: SET lock:seat:42 (NX, EX 10s)
  R-->>B: Lock Acquired (User 1)
  B->>+D: INSERT INTO bookings (seat_id, status='HELD', expires_at=NOW()+10m)
  D-->>-B: Hold Recorded
  B-->>C1: 200 OK { hold_id: "h_99", expires_in: 600 }

  B->>R: Attempt lock for User 2
  R-->>-B: Lock Failed (Key exists)
  B-->>C2: 409 Conflict (Seat currently held by another user)

  opt Payment Timeout Exceeded
    Note over W,D: Background Worker scans expired holds
    W->>+D: UPDATE bookings SET status='EXPIRED' WHERE status='HELD' AND expires_at < NOW()
    D-->>-W: Released expired seats
  end

notes.sequence:
## Concurrency Control in Ticket Booking
- Distributed lock via Redis `SET NX EX` guarantees mutual exclusion.
- Loser of the lock race receives an immediate 409 Conflict.
- Background worker reclaims abandoned holds without manual intervention.

solution.explanation: Resolves concurrent race conditions using atomic distributed locking in Redis and handles temporary holds with automatic worker-driven expiration.
solution.approach: Atomic distributed lock pattern with TTL-based state machine.
